sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Ọba** (*oba*) — River, Devotion, Sanctuary · The river orisha Ọba — co-wife of the thunder god, lady of the sacred waters — belongs to the Yoruba tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "River, Devotion, Sanctuary". The name means "The river orisha Ọba — co-wife of the thunder god, lady of the sacred waters"[^1].

Ọba is the river orisha who loved and lost: the third and most senior wife of Ṣàngó, whose jealousy cost her an ear and whose grief became a lake. She is the Yoruba study of endurance — the quiet river that outlasts the storm-god's louder wives.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Ọba** and serves its temple at [ọba.com](https://xn--ba-58s.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *oba* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.
E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.
Abraham (biblical patriarch / Genesis narrative), Book of Genesis, 1000 BCE.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Ọba** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "The river orisha Ọba — co-wife of the thunder god, lady of the sacred waters"[^1].

The ASCII form *oba* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Ọba** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **o** → **Ọ** — Open-mid o with underdot
- **b** → **b** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

The project holds the domain **ọba.com** (xn--ba-58s.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.
E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ɔ̀.bá/** — Standard Yoruba.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: aw-BAH — open o, low-high melody.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Yoruba** — Ọ̀bá
- **Cuba (Santería)** — Obá
- **Owned form** — Ọba

Ọba names the river orisha of the Ọba River; the precomposed dot-below Ọ is the domain-maximal form (tone marks cannot be registered), and the fuller tone-marked Ọ̀bá is preserved in the temple's display text. The dot-below marks the open-mid vowel; the fuller tonal form Ọ̀bá is preserved in the temple's display text.

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual yoruba names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Ọba** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Ọba is the river orisha who loved and lost: the third and most senior wife of Ṣàngó, whose jealousy cost her an ear and whose grief became a lake. She is the Yoruba study of endurance — the quiet river that outlasts the storm-god's louder wives.[^1]

### The Ọba River

Her water in Yorubaland — the stream that bears her name and her temperament.

### The Hidden Ear

The ear she lost to Ṣàngó's rage — hidden under her crown and her hair.

### The Senior Wife

First among the three — and last to be believed.

### The Lake

Her grief made geography: the lake where the faithful mourn with her.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Ọba concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The covered ear** — Wounds hidden and endured — dignity after injury
- **The brass bracelet** — Her marriage-token from the thunder-king
- **The red parrot feather** — Her sign beside the other wives' red

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Ọba's myths are domestic tragedy told as hydrology: the co-wife's war that became a river and a lake.[^1]

### Three Wives, One Storm (The Rivalry)

Ṣàngó, the thunder-king, took three river-wives: Ọba the senior, Ọṣun the beloved, and Ọya the storm-sharer. The oríkì tell how Ọba, seeing her husband's love flow to Ọṣun, schemed — and how Ọṣun, learning of it, tricked her in return: she told Ọba the king loved the ear of a woman in his soup, and Ọba, desperate to be loved, cut her own ear and cooked it for him.[^2]

### The Ear in the Soup (The Rage)

When the trick was revealed, Ṣàngó's disgust and rage drove her from the palace; the co-wives laughed, and Ọba fled north, weeping. She hid her maimed head under her crown and her hair — which is why her images cover the ears — and the thunder-king, in the later tellings, never stopped regretting the day. Her myth is the Yoruba warning about jealousy: not the villain's punishment, but the victim's endurance.

### The Water of Her Grief (The Lake)

Her tears became her realm: the Ọba River and the lake of her worship, where her priests keep her cult to this day. The co-wives' war never ended — Ọba and Ọya still cannot be honored in the same shrine — but her people say the senior wife outlasted them: storms pass, the river stays. The crown that hides her ear is her whole theology: dignity is what you keep when you have lost what you loved.

sources.citation: E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, Longmans, Green & Co., 1962.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
In Cuba's Santería she is Obá, syncretized with Santa Catalina de Alejandría (Saint Catherine, whose wheel she shares) — her cult strong in Matanzas; in Brazil's Candomblé, Obá keeps her river and her covered ear, the devotee-dancers' hair arranged to hide what the king did. The three-wife cycle (Ọba-Ọṣun-Ọya) is the diaspora's standard parable of the polygamous household, told wherever the orisha went.[^1]

Within the Yoruba tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aganju|Aganjú]], [[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]], [[eshu|Ẹṣu]], [[obatala|Ọbatálá]], [[ogun|Ògún]], and [[olodumare|Olódùmarè]].

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Her image — the crowned figure hiding her ears — is one of Yoruba art's most intimate: the wound as regalia. The co-wives' cycle structures the orisha households of two continents; her river in Yorubaland keeps her shrines active; and the "Obá" of Cuban Santería is beloved as the most patient of the female orisha — the one who teaches that endurance is also a form of power.[^1]

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Her river rises in the hills of the Ọyọ country, and her cult-centers at Ọṣogbo and the Ọba lake preserve her shrines and her priests; the brass and terracotta figures of the covered-ear goddess are documented in the museum collections from Ifẹ̀ to Havana. The oríkì of the three wives, recorded by Bascom and others, is among the finest domestic myth-cycles in the Yoruba corpus.[^1]

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.

sections.label: Ifá Corpus
sections.body: The Ifá corpus knows the co-wives' war: the odù that tell of Ṣàngó's household use Ọba's story as the divination-canon's standing warning on jealousy — the senior wife's maiming recited as the proof that envy wounds the envier. The babaláwo cite her ear in the counseling of households: the oracle that answers polygamy's oldest question with the river that outlasted the storm.

sources.citation: Bascom, Ifa Divination (the co-wives odù).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Oral Tradition
sections.body: Her oríkì are the river's own elegy: the praise-names — "senior wife of the thunder," "she who hides her ear and keeps her crown," "the river that endures" — and the Ọba River traditions of her flight and her lake. The oral cycle of the three wives, told at the Ọṣogbo shrines and in the hunters' guilds, is among the finest domestic myth-cycles in the Yoruba archive: the palace as weather, the river as the one who stays.

sources.citation: Idowu, Olodumare (Ogun and river oríkì); the Ọba shrine traditions.

sections.label: Diaspora Traditions
sections.body: In Cuba she is **Obá** of Santería — syncretized with Santa Catalina, her cult strong at Matanzas, her priests arranging the devotee's hair over the covered ear; in Brazil's Candomblé she keeps her river and her dignity. The diaspora kept the cycle whole: Ọba, Ọṣun, Ọya, three rivers, one storm — the New World's orisha households recite her as the patron of the patient: the wife who lost everything and kept the river.

sources.citation: Bascom, Shango in the New World (Obá cults); the Matanzas records.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Ọba is the goddess of what remains when the shouting is over. The storm-wives got the thunder; she got the river — and rivers outlive storms by definition. Her crown covers her ear, not her shame: the difference is everything. She asks the question the senior wife knows best: after the injustice, what do you cover, what do you keep, and what do you let become a lake?

The priests say her crown was made to her own design, after the flight — the first piece of jewelry in the corpus that exists to hide a wound and to honor it at once. Everyone who has dressed carefully on a difficult morning knows her liturgy. The river does not hide; it covers, and continues.

The co-wives' war never officially ends in the tellings — Ọba and Ọya still cannot share a shrine — and that honesty is the corpus' gift: reconciliation is not mandatory, but endurance is possible. Her lake holds its annual mourners quietly, without demanding anyone forgive. The river just keeps being a river, which is the last word of every telling.

The priests arrange the devotee's hair the same way she arranged hers — forward, covering — and the gesture has crossed four hundred years and an ocean intact. In Matanzas they say her patience is the kind the world does not notice until it is the only thing left standing. The thunder made his point; the river is still making hers.

Her lake keeps what the palace could not: a congregation that has never once asked her to be anyone else. The covered ear, the crown, the river, the patience — the whole of her is a single sentence, and it reads the same in Ọṣogbo and Matanzas: endurance is not surrender; it is sovereignty, kept quietly, until the storm runs out of thunder.

The storm-wives write the loud chapters; she writes the long one. And long chapters are the ones the grandchildren keep.

The river does not argue its case. It simply arrives, season after season, until the whole valley agrees: the quiet one was the permanent one all along.[^1]

sources.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana University Press, 1969.
